questions.prompt: What is a language model actually doing when it answers you?
options: Looking up the answer in a large database of checked facts it was given
Predicting the words most likely to follow, from patterns in its training text
Searching the web live and summarising the most relevant pages it finds
Working out your goal and reasoning about it step by step as a person would
questions.explanation: A language model predicts what comes next. That one fact explains most of its strange behaviour, from invented citations to generic answers.

questions.prompt: A model gives you a source that turns out not to exist. Why does that happen?
options: The source existed once but was deleted after the model was trained
The model has been told to invent sources to make answers look stronger
The answer was cut short, so the real source never finished loading
A realistic citation is what usually follows that kind of sentence
questions.explanation: The model produces what plausibly comes next. A realistic-looking citation is plausible whether or not it is real, which is why sources always need checking.

questions.prompt: What was introduced in 2017 that every model you use today descends from?
options: The transformer, from "Attention Is All You Need"
The Turing test, from "Computing Machinery and Intelligence"
ChatGPT, released to the public by OpenAI that November
The chatbot ELIZA, rebuilt with a much larger vocabulary
questions.explanation: The transformer came in 2017. ChatGPT arrived five years later and gave it a text box, which is why so many people think the story starts in 2022.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between chat and an agent?
options: Chat is free to use; an agent only works on a paid plan with credits
An agent is a chatbot that has been given a much larger memory to use
Chat gives you an answer; an agent takes a goal and returns finished work
Chat runs on your laptop; an agent always runs on a company's server
questions.explanation: With chat you get advice and do the job yourself. An agent takes a goal and does the work: files written, pages built, checks run.

questions.prompt: What three steps does Claude Code repeat until a goal is met?
options: Read the prompt, write one answer, then wait for your next message
Gather context, take action, then verify the results of what it did
Search the web, summarise the pages, then save a report file for you
Ask you a question, pick a model, then choose the fastest tool to use
questions.explanation: Every agent loops through gathering context, taking action and verifying results, often many times on one task.

questions.prompt: Which goal gives an agent a clear point to stop?
options: "Build a price list page. It is done when every price reads on a phone."
"Build me a nice price list page for my cake business, and make it good."
"Build a price list page and keep improving it until it looks perfect."
"Build a price list page, and just use your best judgement on the rest."
questions.explanation: "It is done when..." gives the agent a finish line it can check. Vague goals get vague stopping points.

questions.prompt: An agent starts forgetting rules you gave it early in a long session. What is the best fix?
options: Repeat every rule at the top of each new message in the same long chat
Keep the session open for longer so it has time to catch back up again
Switch to another model and paste the whole conversation into it again
Put the rules in CLAUDE.md and start a fresh session for each new goal
questions.explanation: When a session fills up, older instructions can get lost. CLAUDE.md is read at the start of every session, so rules there survive a fresh start.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a prompt and a skill?
options: A prompt works in any chat tool; a skill only works inside Claude Code itself
A skill is just a longer prompt that you save and paste in at the start of a chat
A prompt is what you type; a skill holds a recurring job so you stop typing it
A prompt is for one-off questions; a skill is for questions with a single right answer
questions.explanation: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file holding the instructions for one recurring job. The model reads it when that job comes up, so your corrections survive between conversations.

questions.prompt: Your skill works when you open it directly, but the model never uses it on its own. What is the most likely cause?
options: The description does not use the words you type for that job
The instructions are too short for the model to follow them
Skills only switch on for people who are on a paid plan
Having more than one skill installed makes them all stop
questions.explanation: At first the model reads only each skill's name and description. The description is a trigger, not a summary, so it has to use the words you really type.

questions.prompt: Which line in a skill is most likely to change the output?
options: "You are a world-class copywriter."
"Write clearly and professionally."
"Always do your very best work."
"Never use the word leverage."
questions.explanation: Specific bans beat any amount of positive description. "Write clearly" is a wish. "Never use the word leverage" is a rule the model can follow.
